turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A mechanical watch has dozens of moving parts, but it uses only a few drops of oil. In fact, the total amount is so small that you could barely see it. Yet those tiny drops are essential.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Wherever two parts move against each other, there is friction. Friction wastes energy and causes wear. Oil reduces both. The places where a watchmaker adds oil are called lubrication points. Each one has its own needs.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: For example, the pivots of fast-moving wheels need a very thin oil. Parts that carry heavy loads, like the mainspring, need thicker oils or greases. The escapement, which works thousands of times every hour, often needs a special oil of its own. So one watch may use four or five different synthetic oils. Synthetic oils are made in a laboratory. They last longer and stay more stable than natural oils.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Putting oil in the right place is a skill. The watchmaker uses a tool called an oiler, which is like a tiny needle. Too little oil, and the part wears out. Too much, and the oil spreads to places where it should not be.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: To help keep the oil in place, many jewel holes have a small cup shape around them, called an oil sink. Surface tension holds the drop there, like water in a small dish.
